docs.title: Human Superintelligence Readiness Index (HSRI)
docs.text: Project Status: Early Research Feasibility Draft — Not Peer Reviewed. Audience & Purpose: Academic, think tank, AI policy, and corporate R&D reviewers evaluating construct validity, measurement feasibility, and index governance.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Human Superintelligence Readiness Index (HSRI) is a research feasibility inquiry assessing whether human psychological, cognitive, and behavioral readiness for increasingly capable artificial intelligence can be scientifically measured and indexed.

Core Empirical Finding: Human Superintelligence Readiness (HSR) is not a new psychological faculty. Every candidate sub-component—attentional control, metacognition, decision agency, value clarity, AI literacy, and calibrated trust—already possesses an established, validated literature base. The genuine, narrow research gap is whether these substrates, measured jointly and specifically under interaction with an AI system whose task performance meets or exceeds the person's own, predict outcomes that separate instruments do not already explain. That is a testable empirical hypothesis, not yet an established construct.

Headline Recommendation: DEVELOP AS A RESEARCH CONSTRUCT FIRST. Not "develop now" (no validation data exists, and public indexing risks are unmanaged), and not "concept not sufficiently distinct" (a defensible, narrow integration gap exists once the construct is restricted to AI-interaction behavior).

Epistemic Standard: Because this is a feasibility assessment about a proposed scientific construct, it holds itself strictly to scientific auditability: - Every effect size, citation, and experimental parameter is either traceable to a verified peer-reviewed source or explicitly marked as illustrative or unverified ([UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE]). - Spurious precision (e.g., invented decimal effect sizes or fabricated hallucination rates) has been deliberately removed. - Claims are categorized into five transparent evidence tiers, with full audit trails cataloged in the Master Evidence Table.

docs.title: Why Human Superintelligence Readiness Matters
docs.text:
For decades, international technology-readiness frameworks (such as network infrastructure indices, digital economy benchmarks, and government AI-readiness indices) have measured compute, bandwidth, and capital adoption, implicitly assuming that human agency remains sovereign and technology acts as a passive amplifier of human intent. As AI systems advance toward general-purpose reasoning, drafting, planning, and autonomous execution, that sovereignty assumption weakens in four specific, testable failure modes:

  1. Cognitive Offloading and Deskilling: Well-established for memory and navigation tasks (transactive-memory effects with search engines and GPS navigation); the extension to active synthesis, argumentation, and code generation by generative AI is a live, active research question rather than a settled finding.
  2. Automation Complacency Under Fluent Output: Confident, fluent, syntactically correct AI output frequently appears more trustworthy than it is, triggering well-documented automation bias and reducing independent analytical verification.
  3. Value and Goal Drift Under Optimization: The hypothesis that AI's expanding capability to optimize means increases human reliance on explicit clarity about ends is philosophically coherent but currently empirically untested.
  4. Trust Miscalibration in Both Directions: Populations lacking calibrated trust either over-rely on automated advice (misuse) or reflexively reject valid machine assistance (disuse)—a dynamic documented across decades of automation literature predating modern generative models.

Critically, investigating these failure modes does not require assuming that artificial general intelligence or superintelligence will emerge. It requires only that AI systems already outperform individual humans at specific, high-frequency cognitive tasks—a reality observable today in chess engines, diagnostic classifiers, forecasting models, and code-synthesis agents.

docs.title: Epistemic Standards and Evidence Tiers
docs.text:
To allow rapid scrutiny by skeptical reviewers, claims across this repository are tagged using a five-tier taxonomy:

Tier Tag Meaning & Standard Tier 1: Strong {: .evidence-strong } Multiple converging peer-reviewed sources; replicated empirical findings; multi-decade consensus literatures. Tier 2: Moderate {: .evidence-moderate } Single high-quality randomized controlled trial (RCT), meta-analysis with caveats, or small consistent literature. Tier 3: Preliminary {: .evidence-preliminary } Active, recent research area (e.g., 2020–2026 generative AI studies); findings replicate across limited contexts. Tier 4: Theoretical {: .evidence-theoretical } Coherent logical, mathematical, or philosophical argument without direct empirical testing in an AI-specific setting. Tier 5: Speculative {: .evidence-speculative } Plausible extrapolation or scenario framing; currently outside empirical reach. Unverified [UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE] Claim appears in source materials without an identifiable, checked empirical citation.

All empirical claims are indexed in the Master Evidence Table, detailing claim text, page references, evidence tier, citations, and DOI/URL links.

docs.title: Repository and Report Structure
docs.text:
This documentation is structured into nine sequential analytical sections:

  1. Definition and Scope: Operational definition, candidate definitions comparison, explicit boundary exclusions, and capability levels A through F.
  2. Existing Global Indices: Methodological review of HDI, SPI, World Happiness Report, MPI, GII/GKI, documented criticisms, and four architectural lessons for HSRI.
  3. Construct Redundancy Audit: Systematic mapping against validated psychological constructs, automation bias literature, cognitive forcing functions, and contemplative science.
  4. Causal Model and Index Design: Human agency as the organizing axis, 4-tier conceptual scaffold, indicator retention decisions, and aggregation models (individual, organizational, national).
  5. Measurement and Experiments: Multi-method measurement strategy and nine standardized behavioral human-AI interaction experiments.
  6. Cross-Cultural Validity and Ethics: Measurement invariance requirements, eight ethical failure modes (including responsibility laundering), and governance charters.
  7. Objections and Counterarguments: Rigorous analysis of eleven major counterarguments, evaluated without defensive smoothing.
  8. Research Roadmap: 11-phase research sequence (Phases 0–10), gating criteria, and the top ten open research gaps.
  9. Final Recommendation: Core verdict, model selection, precise next pre-registered experiment, and reading list.

docs.title: 1. Definition and Scope
docs.text: A scientific index requires a falsifiable construct with explicit boundary conditions. Informal definitions of "AI readiness" frequently conflate inputs, cognitive processes, and normative outcomes into vague wellness or maturity labels that resist empirical disconfirmation. This section establishes the operational definition, evaluates alternative formulations, articulates explicit boundary exclusions, and specifies the capability framework within which the construct operates.

docs.title: 1.1 Candidate Definitions Compared
docs.text:
To clarify construct boundaries, four candidate formulations were systematically evaluated against psychometric criteria:

Candidate Formulation Conceptual Clarity Construct Novelty Measurability Empirical Support Cultural Neutrality Pseudoscience Risk A. General maturity: "The general psychological and cognitive maturity of a person or society in the AI era." Low Very Low (collapses into flourishing) Low N/A (too diffuse to test) Low High B. Future-event readiness: "A person's readiness for the eventual arrival of superintelligent AI." Low Low Very Low (predicated on an undefined future milestone) None Medium High C. Input composite: "The composite of psychological stability, metacognition, agency, value clarity, and AI literacy that predicts preserved human agency when interacting with capable AI." Medium-High Medium Medium-High Preliminary (component substrates validated separately) Medium (requires cross-cultural testing) Moderate (manageable with psychometric controls) D. Behavioral interaction (Recommended): "The demonstrated behavioral capacity to maintain calibrated trust, independent judgment, and value-directed goal-setting when interacting with AI systems whose task-specific performance meets or exceeds one's own." High Medium-High (anchors to observable interaction rather than future forecasting) High (operationalizable via behavioral performance tasks) Preliminary but empirically testable today Medium Low (anchored in present, observable asymmetry)

Candidate D avoids the definitional trap of predicting hypothetical technological milestones, instead isolating an observable psychological dynamic.

docs.title: 1.2 Recommended Operational Definition
docs.text:
Human Superintelligence Readiness (HSRI Operational Definition): The demonstrated behavioral capacity of an individual, organization, or society to maintain calibrated trust, independent judgment, and value-directed goal-setting when interacting with AI systems whose task-specific performance meets or exceeds their own — measured behaviorally wherever possible, not merely self-reported.

This definition deliberately anchors "readiness" to present-day, observable cognitive asymmetry (such as an individual interacting with a chess engine, diagnostic classifier, forecasting system, or code-generation agent) rather than an unproven future technological event. The term "superintelligence" is retained in the project's public title strictly as an aspirational scenario framing device, not as an empirical precondition.

docs.title: 1.3 Explicit Boundary Exclusions
docs.text:
To prevent construct creep, HSRI explicitly excludes six commonly confused concepts:

Excluded Concept Common Misconception Methodological Reason for Exclusion General Intelligence (IQ) Assumed that higher cognitive ability guarantees immune response to AI error. High cognitive ability does not prevent automation bias; fluent reasoners can rationalize erroneous machine outputs just as fluently as correct outputs. AI Literacy & Technical Skill Equated with psychological readiness and discernment. Understanding model architectures or prompt engineering does not confer psychological immunity to persuasion, sycophancy, or over-reliance; technical literacy is a necessary but insufficient substrate. General Mental Health & Happiness Equated with flourishing and cognitive sovereignty. An emotionally stable, satisfied individual can readily surrender decisional autonomy to an agreeable, highly capable AI assistant. Technological Infrastructure Equated with compute availability, broadband speed, and device access. Measures physical capital and institutional adoption, which are distinct from individual cognitive discernment and decisional agency. Belief in Superintelligence Equated with being "prepared" for advanced AI. Readiness is measured against observable task performance; ideological conviction or fear regarding hypothetical future AGI introduces confounding variance rather than diagnostic signal. Contemplative/Meditation Frequency Equated with attentional readiness and mindfulness. Meditation is at most a candidate training intervention for an underlying substrate (executive attention); treating a specific behavioral practice as an outcome metric constitutes a category error.

docs.title: 1.4 The Capability-Level Framework
docs.text:
To establish empirical scope boundaries, human-AI interaction is classified into six ascending capability tiers:

Capability Tier System Operational Role Human Capabilities That Gain Marginal Value Human Capabilities That Lose Marginal Value Primary Behavioral Failure Mode Empirical Feasibility Status Level A: Tool Executes deterministic, explicit human instructions. Basic digital literacy, instruction syntax. Rote manual calculation. Non-adoption. Established / Historical. Level B: Cognitive Assistant Drafts, summarizes, searches, and retrieves information. Verification habits, prompt framing, source checking. Manual information retrieval and preliminary formatting. Mild over-reliance on conversational convenience. Established / Current. Level C: Capable Collaborator Formulates strategies, options, syntheses, and persuasive arguments. Discernment of subtle error, calibrated trust, value clarity. Initial draft synthesis and baseline solution ideation. Automation complacency; susceptibility to sycophantic framing. Active Empirical Focus (HSRI Core). Level D: Autonomous Task Manager Executes multi-step workflows with intermittent supervision. Oversight design, delegation judgment, accountability retention. Manual execution of routine intermediate processes. Deskilling; diffusion of decisional responsibility. Active Empirical Focus (HSRI Core). Level E: Exceeds Human Reasoning Across Many Domains Consistently outperforms most individuals across most cognitive tasks. Meta-evaluative judgment, value governance, epistemic humility, multi-agent coordination. Individual domain expertise as a primary status marker. Identity disruption; systemic epistemic dependence. Preliminary / Cautious Extrapolation. Level F: Hypothetical Superintelligence Radically exceeds collective human cognitive capacity. Unknown; likely requires institutional and societal governance mechanisms beyond individual psychology. Individual cognitive competition. Total cognitive obsolescence or loss of control. Speculative (Outside Current Measurement).

HSRI can be empirically grounded through Level D and cautiously extrapolated to Level E. Level F is retained exclusively as an orienting conceptual horizon, entirely outside what can be measured or validated using contemporary behavioral instruments.

docs.title: 2. Existing Global Indices: Comparative Methodology and Lessons
docs.text: Composite international indices offer vital methodological precedents and structural warnings for designing the Human Superintelligence Readiness Index (HSRI). International index construction has evolved through three distinct historical paradigms, with HSRI positioned provisionally within an unproven fourth.

docs.title: 2.1 Three Historical Paradigms of International Indices
docs.text:
1. Unidimensional Economic Output (Mid-20th Century): Dominated by Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Gross National Product (GNP). While standardized, this paradigm was widely criticized for treating aggregate market activity as synonymous with societal welfare, ignoring distribution, externalities, and non-market capabilities.
  2. Multidimensional Human Capability (1990s): Inaugurated by Mahbub ul-Haq and Amartya Sen through the UNDP's Human Development Index (HDI). Grounded in Sen's capabilities approach, development was redefined as the expansion of substantive human freedoms and capabilities (health, education, purchasing power) rather than income alone.
  3. Deprivation, Governance, and Sustainability (2000s–Present): Represented by the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), the Social Progress Index (SPI), and environmental governance frameworks. These introduced non-compensatory aggregation rules, dual-cutoff identification of deprivation, and explicit measurement of institutional outcomes independent of economic growth.
  4. Cognitive and Epistemic Agency Under AI Asymmetry (Proposed 4th Paradigm): HSRI provisionally sits here—measuring individual- and population-level cognitive discernment, calibrated trust, and preserved decisional agency under interaction with intelligent systems. However, each previous paradigm required more than a decade of contested methodological debate to achieve legitimacy; HSRI cannot assume acceptance without equivalent empirical scrutiny.

docs.title: 2.2 Comparative Methodological Review
docs.text:
The table below examines the mathematical formulation, indicator structure, aggregation methods, and documented critiques of the primary international benchmarks:

Index Sponsoring Organization / Authors Core Dimensions & Indicators Aggregation Mathematics Documented Methodological Criticisms Human Development Index (HDI) UNDP (Mahbub ul-Haq & Amartya Sen, 1990) Health (life expectancy), Education (mean/expected years), Income (GNI per capita). Geometric mean of normalized sub-indices: $$\text{HDI} = (I_{\text{health}} \times I_{\text{education}} \times I_{\text{income}})^{1/3}$$ Ignores net wealth distribution, quality-of-service differences, and environmental sustainability. Companion indices (IHDI, GII, MPI) were required to address inequality and multi-deprivation. Social Progress Index (SPI) Social Progress Imperative (Porter, Stern, & Green, 2013–2017) 3 dimensions (Basic Needs, Foundations of Wellbeing, Opportunity) comprising 12 components and ~50 indicators. Component indicators combined via Principal Component Analysis (PCA); the 12 components themselves are explicitly equal-weighted. Equal weighting of the 12 components assumes each contributes identically and independently to social progress—an assumption with no statistical or theoretical justification (Jitmaneeroj, 2017). Criticized for encoding Western liberal normative assumptions. World Happiness Report UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network (Helliwell, Layard, & Sachs) Cantril ladder life evaluations regressed on GDP, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity, perceptions of corruption. Pooled Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression of national life evaluations against six determinant categories. Correlational rather than causal; relies on a single-item subjective evaluation; deliberately avoids normative definitions of societal structure. Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) Oxford Poverty & Human Development Initiative (OPHI) / UNDP (Alkire & Foster, 2011) 10 indicators across Health, Education, and Living Standards. Non-compensatory dual-cutoff counting method: individuals are identified as poor only if deprived across a weighted threshold ($k$). Deprivation cutoffs ($z_j$) and overall poverty threshold ($k$) are normatively selected rather than empirically derived. Weighting of indicators within dimensions remains contestable. Global Innovation Index (GII) WIPO / Cornell / INSEAD 7 pillars (Institutions, Human capital, Infrastructure, Market/Business sophistication, Knowledge/Creative outputs). Arithmetic mean of equal-weighted pillar scores. Overlap between "input" and "output" pillars creates conceptual collinearity and risks tautological scoring.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Equal-Weighting Fallacy
docs.text: Equal weighting is the most prevalent methodological shortcut in composite index design, yet it remains the primary target of external econometric critique. As Jitmaneeroj (2017) demonstrated regarding the Social Progress Index, equal weighting assumes that every constituent dimension exerts an identical, orthogonal contribution to the latent construct. In reality, sub-dimensions exhibit substantial collinearity and differential predictive power. For HSRI, adopting equal weighting past the initial exploratory pilot would undermine scientific credibility.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Non-Compensatory vs. Compensatory Aggregation
docs.text: Standard arithmetic averaging allows compensatory substitution: an exceptionally high score on one dimension fully offsets a catastrophic failure on another. In the context of human-AI interaction, this formulation is dangerous. If a decision-maker exhibits a near-total inability to detect confident machine hallucinations or an uncritical willingness to surrender oversight, high scores in general AI literacy or abstract value clarity should not mask that critical operational vulnerability. The non-compensatory, dual-cutoff framework of Alkire & Foster (2011) provides the correct psychometric precedent.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Western Normative Bias in Universal Indices
docs.text: The Social Progress Index has faced sustained criticism that its Opportunity dimension reflects predominantly Western normative ideals, systematically penalizing non-Western governance models. Because constructs like "individual autonomy," "agency," and "self-determination" are culturally sensitive, HSRI faces an even greater risk of cultural parochialism if deployed globally without rigorous measurement invariance testing.

docs.title: 2.4 Four Architectural Lessons for HSRI
docs.text:
1. Mandatory Profile Reporting: Never publish a single composite figure without disaggregated sub-scores. Composite point estimates obscure vital structural deficits.
  2. Provisional-to-Empirical Weighting Transition: Equal weighting should be used strictly during exploratory pilot phases, explicitly labeled provisional, and replaced with empirically estimated regression or factor weights following validation studies.
  3. Non-Compensatory Critical-Weakness Floor: Foundational cognitive substrates (such as attentional control and error detection) must operate as non-compensatory thresholds, capping overall readiness when a severe deficiency is detected.
  4. Pre-Registered Invariance Standards: Follow the OECD/JRC Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (2008), pre-registering sensitivity analyses and uncertainty intervals for all aggregation and normalization parameters.

docs.title: 3. Construct Redundancy Audit
docs.text: A central vulnerability of newly proposed psychological indices is construct proliferation (also known as the "jangle fallacy")—attaching a novel label to an existing, well-validated psychological attribute without demonstrating empirical distinctiveness or incremental predictive validity. This section conducts a rigorous redundancy audit of every candidate HSRI component against established cognitive science, human factors, and human-computer interaction literatures.

docs.title: 3.1 Systematic Construct Redundancy Audit
docs.text:
Every candidate dimension proposed in early HSRI concept drafts was audited against established instruments and psychometric literature:

Proposed Dimension Existing Psychological / Cognitive Construct Validated Instrument or Experimental Paradigm Redundancy Verdict Methodological Disposition for HSRI Attentional Control Executive Attention / Sustained Attention Attention Network Test (ANT); Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) Redundant Construct Reusable measurement paradigm; evaluate distraction resistance under AI-driven alerts. Metacognition / Self-Knowledge Metacognitive Monitoring / Sensitivity Confidence-accuracy calibration curves; type-2 signal detection ($meta\text{-}d'$) (Fleming & Lau, 2014) Redundant Construct Direct methodological reuse; calibrate subjective confidence against actual AI output accuracy. Cognitive Flexibility Task-Switching / Set-Shifting Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST); Trail Making Test B Redundant Construct Exclude from core; retain as baseline cognitive covariate. Epistemic Humility Intellectual Humility Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale (Leary et al., 2017) Redundant Construct Direct instrument reuse; captures willingness to revise beliefs when confronted with valid AI evidence. Cognitive Reflection Reflective vs. Intuitive Cognitive Processing Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT; Frederick, 2005) Redundant Construct Useful baseline, but high test-retest familiarity contamination limits repeated longitudinal deployment. Uncertainty Tolerance Intolerance of Uncertainty Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12; Carleton et al., 2007) Redundant Construct Direct instrument reuse; predicts premature surrender of judgment under ambiguous AI recommendations. Decision Agency Autonomous Motivation / Locus of Control Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction Scale (Deci & Ryan); Rotter's I-E Scale Redundant General Construct General construct is mature, but behavioral delegation and override under AI advice is an active empirical gap. Value Clarity & Meaning Goal Contents / Meaning in Life Meaning in Life Questionnaire (MLQ); Portrait Values Questionnaire (Schwartz) Redundant Construct Mature general psychometrics; causal connection to AI optimization remains theoretical. AI Literacy Multi-dimensional AI Competency AI Literacy Questionnaire (Ng et al., 2024); UNESCO Frameworks (2024); OECD/EC Framework (2026) Fully Redundant Field Import wholesale. Active, mature field; HSRI should not reinvent AI literacy measurement. Resistance to Automation Bias / Calibrated Trust Automation Bias; Appropriate Trust & Reliance Errors of omission/commission paradigm (Mosier & Skitka, 1996); trust calibration models (Lee & See, 2004) Fully Redundant Construct Mature in classical automation (aviation, medicine); extension to generative/agentic AI is the genuine research frontier.

Audit Conclusion: Virtually all proposed sub-constructs are redundant with established, peer-reviewed psychology. The sole defensible, non-redundant scientific contribution lies in measuring how these established cognitive substrates function jointly under interaction with adaptive, persuasive, generative AI counterparts—an interactive environment that static psychometric batteries (such as standard Stroop or card-sorting tasks) do not replicate.

docs.title: 3.2 Human-AI Interaction: Automation Bias, Reliance, and Calibrated Trust
docs.text: The foundational literature on automated decision aids spans three decades of empirical validation:

docs.title: 3.2.1 Automation Stages and Levels
docs.text: Parasuraman, Sheridan, and Wickens (2000) formalized a four-stage framework of human interaction with automation: (1) information acquisition, (2) information analysis, (3) decision selection, and (4) action implementation. Their empirical synthesis established that automating the decision selection stage produces the greatest degree of human operator complacency, cognitive disengagement, and loss of situational awareness.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Errors of Omission and Commission
docs.text: Mosier and Skitka (1996) demonstrated that automation bias manifests through two distinct failure modes: - Errors of Omission: Operators fail to notice system hazards or critical anomalies because automated monitoring aids did not trigger an alert. - Errors of Commission: Operators follow an incorrect automated recommendation even when contradictory evidence is directly available in the physical environment.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Trust Calibration vs. Subjective Trust
docs.text:
Lee and See (2004) formalized trust calibration: trust is calibrated when an operator's subjective confidence matches the actual operational capability of the automated system. They identified two failure states: - Overtrust (Misuse): Operator trust exceeds system capability, leading to uncritical reliance and automation bias. - Undertrust (Disuse): System capability exceeds operator trust, resulting in reflexive rejection of valid advice (algorithm aversion).

A 2025 PRISMA-compliant systematic review synthesizing 35 peer-reviewed studies (2015–2025) confirmed that automation bias manifests across modern AI-driven enterprise workflows, proving that the phenomenon extends into contemporary machine-learning environments rather than being restricted to legacy aviation systems.

docs.title: 3.3 The Failure of Explanations and the Role of Cognitive Forcing Functions
docs.text: A critical design insight from recent empirical human-AI interaction research concerns the limitations of model transparency and explainable AI (XAI):

docs.title: 3.3.1 Transparency Can Increase Over-Reliance
docs.text: Bansal et al. (2021, CHI) demonstrated that providing AI explanations does not reliably improve complementary human-AI team performance. In multiple experimental conditions, adding local feature-importance explanations increased operator over-reliance on incorrect machine recommendations, because fluent, plausible explanations created an illusion of system competence.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Cognitive Forcing Functions Reduce Automation Bias
docs.text:
Buçinca, Malaya, and Gajos (2021, CSCW) evaluated interventions to mitigate over-reliance. They demonstrated that while passive explanation interfaces failed, cognitive forcing functions—design interventions that compel deliberate, active analytical judgment before an AI recommendation is revealed or accepted (such as requiring the user to formulate and commit to an independent hypothesis first)—statistically significantly reduced over-reliance. Furthermore, this intervention effect was moderated by individual Need for Cognition (NFC): participants with higher baseline motivation for cognitive effort benefited significantly more from forced deliberation.

This finding directly informs HSRI's behavioral experimental battery: static self-report cannot measure resistance to automation bias; diagnostic validity requires behavioral paradigms that test whether individuals engage deliberative verification under fluent machine prompting.

docs.title: 3.4 Cognitive Offloading and Deskilling
docs.text:
Cognitive offloading—the practice of using physical actions or external artifacts to reduce cognitive demands (Risko & Gilbert, 2016)—is well-documented in human cognition. Transactive memory research has demonstrated offloading effects in search engine usage and spatial navigation via GPS systems.

However, the hypothesized extension of this effect to high-order analytical synthesis, critical argumentation, and conceptual reasoning under generative AI remains an active empirical hypothesis without robust longitudinal validation. High-quality longitudinal studies demonstrating irreversible cognitive deskilling from LLM usage do not yet exist. In HSRI, generative deskilling must be classified as a research gap, not a verified finding.

docs.title: 3.5 Contemplative Science: Empirical Review and Boundary Delimitation
docs.text:
Early conceptual drafts of HSRI proposed including meditation practice frequency as an indicator of attentional and psychological readiness. A rigorous review of the contemplative science literature demonstrates that this represents an overreach:

Empirical Claim Evidence Base Effect Size & Statistical Parameters Strength Tier Methodological Caveats & Assessment Mindfulness improves executive attention Meta-analyses of Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) Hedges' $g = 0.29$ for intervention studies; $g = 0.32$ comparing long-term meditators to non-meditators (Sumantry & Stewart, 2021). Moderate Effects concentrated narrowly in conflict inhibition / executive control; no general cognitive boost. Mindfulness improves working memory Meta-analysis of RCTs in healthy adults Overall effect $g = 0.20$; non-significant effect on working memory capacity specifically (Yakobi, Smilek, & Danckert, 2021). Weak / Null Executive control shows modest gains, but working memory retention is not reliably altered in healthy populations. Mindfulness improves alerting / orienting networks Systematic reviews of attention sub-networks Small, inconsistent effect sizes across trials (Sharpe, 2021). Weak Doctoral meta-analysis and primary experimental series yielded non-significant or null effects on alerting/orienting networks. Dose-response relationship (sessions vs. hours) Moderation analyses of meditation interventions Number of formal in-class sessions moderates effect size; total accumulated intervention hours does not (Yakobi et al., 2021). Preliminary Authors note that session count may reflect participant motivation and compliance rather than neurobiological dose-response. Broader clinical vs. cognitive outcomes Large-scale comparative systematic review (47 RCTs, $n = 3{,}515$) Moderate evidence for reduction of anxiety (ES = 0.38 at 8 weeks), depression (ES = 0.30), and pain (ES = 0.33); low evidence of any effect on attention specifically (Goyal et al., 2014, JAMA Intern Med). Moderate for Affect; Weak-to-Null for Attention Found no evidence that meditation outperforms active behavioral treatments (exercise, therapy); attention effects were statistically negligible.

docs.title: Contemplative Science Conclusion
docs.text:
Meditation produces small, domain-specific effects on executive attention ($g \approx 0.29$), but the largest and highest-quality comparative meta-analysis (Goyal et al., 2014) identified low evidence for attentional benefits specifically—the precise substrate required for AI discernment.

Therefore, meditation practice must be classified strictly as a candidate training intervention, never as an indicator or constituent dimension of readiness. HSRI must measure attentional control and metacognitive monitoring directly through standardized behavioral tasks (ANT, SART, calibration curves), remaining entirely agnostic to whether an individual trained those faculties through contemplative practice, athletic training, musicianship, or software engineering.

docs.title: 4. Causal Model and Index Design
docs.text: Designing a scientifically defensible index requires an explicit structural theory linking foundational psychological capacities to observable behavioral outcomes under AI cognitive asymmetry. This section outlines human agency as the central organizing axis, articulates a four-tier conceptual scaffold, details dimension retention decisions, evaluates three aggregation architectures, and examines multi-level feasibility across individual, organizational, and national domains.

docs.title: 4.1 Human Agency as the Central Organizing Axis
docs.text:
The core organizing axis of HSRI is agency, not capability or throughput.

Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan), autonomy (acting from reflective volition and internal endorsement) is empirically distinguishable from competence (capability):

  • High Capability / Low Agency: A technical expert who, facing complex code or analytical outputs, reflexively accepts fluent AI recommendations without verification, diffusing personal accountability.
  • Low Capability / High Agency: A non-expert who knowingly delegates task execution to an AI system while retaining full ownership of the criteria for success, critically probing assumptions, and accepting responsibility for failures.

No existing composite capability index (e.g., HDI, Social Progress Index, Human Capital Index) captures this behavioral distinction at the individual level. Concentrating on agency prevents HSRI from collapsing into a conventional cognitive ability test or digital literacy benchmark.

docs.title: 4.2 Proposed Four-Tier Conceptual Framework
docs.text:
To structure empirical investigation, candidate variables are organized into a four-tier theoretical scaffold:

[ Tier 1: Foundational Substrates (Endogenous) ]
  ├── Executive Attentional Control (ANT / SART)
  ├── Metacognitive Sensitivity (Confidence-Accuracy Calibration)
  └── Cognitive Flexibility (Task-Switching / Set-Shifting)
           │
           ▼
[ Tier 2: Higher-Order Epistemic & Decisional Mediators ]
  ├── Cognitive Reflection (CRT)
  ├── Intellectual / Epistemic Humility (CIHS)
  ├── Uncertainty Tolerance (IUS-12)
  └── Value Clarity & Reflective Endorsement (PVQ)
           │
           ▼
[ Tier 3: AI-Interaction Behavioral Interface (Novel Core) ]
  ├── Calibrated Trust & Appropriate Reliance (Reliance Ratio)
  ├── Discernment of Confident-Wrong AI Outputs (Detection Rate)
  ├── Override Latency, Accuracy, and Willingness
  └── Resistance to Persuasive / Sycophantic AI Framing
           │
           ▼
[ Tier 4: Emergent Outcome ]
  └── Preserved Decisional Agency and Value-Directed Goal-Setting

docs.title: Causal Ordering Hypotheses
docs.text:
Foundational substrates (Tier 1) are hypothesized to enable higher-order mediators (Tier 2), which in turn enable specific AI-interaction competencies (Tier 3), collectively predicting preserved agency (Tier 4).

Methodological Epistemic Rule: This four-tier arrangement is a theoretical scaffold to be empirically tested, not a fitted structural equation model. Stating pre-calibrated path coefficients (e.g., $\beta$ or $\gamma$ weights) prior to data collection conveys false mathematical precision and introduces pseudoscience risk. The required scientific sequence is: (1) establish tiers conceptually and achieve expert consensus via Delphi panels, (2) gather empirical pilot data, and (3) fit and publish structural equation models with transparent standard errors and confidence intervals.

docs.title: 4.3 Candidate Dimensions: Inclusion, Pruning, and Retention
docs.text:
Early proposals contained 18 disparate dimensions. Applying the redundancy audit produced the following pruning decisions:

Candidate Dimension Proposed Tier Methodological Disposition Psychometric Rationale Psychological Stability Baseline Reject as standalone; retain as affective covariate under cognitive load. Standalone measure conflates readiness with general neuroticism and clinical mental health. Attentional Control Tier 1 Retain (Endogenous Substrate) Necessary substrate for resisting notification interruptions and detecting subtle model drift. Metacognition Tier 1 Retain (Monitoring Substrate) Core self-monitoring capacity; confidence-accuracy calibration methods directly reusable. Self-Knowledge — Merge into Metacognition Conceptually redundant with metacognitive monitoring. Cognitive Flexibility Baseline Retain as covariate Required to update priors given valid AI evidence, but fully measured by standard neuropsychological tests. Epistemic Humility Tier 2 Retain (Mediator) Prevents algorithm aversion and dogmatic rejection of valid machine assistance. Discernment Tier 3 Operationalize via Behavioral Tasks Measure behaviorally via detection of confident-wrong outputs rather than via self-report. Decision Agency Tier 4 Retain (Primary Outcome) Central organizing construct of the index. Value Clarity Tier 2 Retain as Theoretical / Supplementary Protects against goal drift toward machine-optimized proxy metrics; empirical link to AI context remains unverified [UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE]. Meaning / Purpose — Move to Supplementary Research Substantial cross-cultural variation; high risk of measurement non-invariance. AI Literacy Tier 3 Retain (Import Frameworks) Import existing validated frameworks (UNESCO, OECD, Ng et al.) rather than creating redundant scales. Generic Collaboration — Reject Conflates preserved human agency with mere operational task throughput. Automation-Bias Resistance Tier 3 Retain (Behavioral Interface) Primary behavioral indicator anchored in decades of human factors literature. Resistance to Manipulation — Merge with Automation-Bias Resistance Driven by identical underlying mechanisms of epistemic vigilance. Uncertainty Tolerance Tier 2 Retain (Mediator) Predicts premature surrender of judgment when facing ambiguous machine recommendations. Accountability Retention Tier 4 Retain (Outcome Dimension) Distinct from override behavior; measures whether an operator accepts moral/causal ownership of AI-assisted outputs. Social / Relational Resilience — Move to Institutional / Societal Level Belongs to organizational governance, not individual psychometrics. Independent Judgment — Merge with Decision Agency Conceptually identical under conditions of cognitive conflict.

docs.title: 4.4 Index Design: Three Candidate Architectures
docs.text:
Evaluating aggregation architectures is critical to avoid structural failure modes documented in existing international indices:

Architecture Model Mathematical Structure Weighting Scheme Architectural Strengths Critical Weaknesses & Failure Modes Model A: Equal-Weight Composite Arithmetic mean of normalized sub-scores: $$I = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k S_i$$ Equal weights assigned a priori ($w_i = 1/k$). Simple, fully transparent, computationally trivial to audit. Inherits the SPI's primary methodological flaw: assumes each component contributes identically and independently to readiness (Jitmaneeroj, 2017). Model B: Evidence-Weighted Composite Weighted sum or regression model: $$I = \sum_{i=1}^k w_i S_i$$ Empirically derived weights (PCA factor loadings or regression coefficients predicting real override accuracy). Statistically defensible; aligns weights with actual predictive power. Premature before Phase 6 validation. Weights cannot be estimated without large-scale validation data; claiming empirical weights today is methodologically fraudulent. Model C: Hierarchical / Threshold Composite Domain profile reporting with non-compensatory critical-weakness floor: $$I = f(\mathbf{S}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \min(S_{\text{Tier 1}}) \ge \theta$$ Foundational domains act as non-compensatory gating constraints; higher tiers aggregated conditionally. Prevents high literacy or confidence from compensating for a total inability to catch critical machine errors. Aligns with MPI dual-cutoff logic (Alkire & Foster, 2011). More complex to communicate; selecting cutoff thresholds ($\theta$) involves normative judgment that requires explicit pre-registration and sensitivity testing.

docs.title: Architectural Recommendation
docs.text: Adopt Model C's reporting logic (disaggregated domain profiles accompanied by critical-weakness flags) while utilizing Model A's provisional equal weighting strictly during exploratory pilot studies (Phase 4). Migrate to Model B's empirical weights only after Phase 6 psychometric validation generates real criterion data.

docs.title: 4.5 Multi-Level Feasibility: Individual, Organizational, National
docs.text:
Analytical Level Scientific Feasibility Recommended Operational Form Critical Methodological Caution Individual HSRI Feasible as Research Instrument Standardized behavioral battery (ANT, calibration tasks, simulated AI-interaction scenarios). Must not be published as public rankings or used for employment screening. Organizational HSRI Feasible as Diagnostic Audit Workflow auditing of override behavior, accountability tracing, and error-recovery latency in real decision systems. Substantially overlaps existing IT change-management and digital-maturity models. National HSRI Not Currently Feasible as Aggregated Psychometrics Separate composite of national indicators: AI curriculum penetration, institutional trust, information integrity, and regulatory governance quality. Aggregating individual psychological scores to national averages commits an ecological fallacy and duplicates established AI-readiness indices.

National benchmarking should not be attempted until Phases 1–6 have rigorously validated the individual construct.

docs.title: 5. Measurement Strategy and Standardized Experiments
docs.text: A core psychometric vulnerability of technology-readiness frameworks is reliance on subjective self-report questionnaires. In psychological domains such as cognitive reflection, overconfidence, and automation bias, self-reports exhibit severe social desirability and Dunning-Kruger biases: individuals most prone to automation complacency frequently evaluate their own vigilance as exceptionally high. To establish scientific credibility, HSRI requires an empirical multi-method measurement strategy centered on standardized behavioral experiments.

docs.title: 5.1 Multi-Method Measurement Architecture
docs.text:
The measurement framework integrates self-report inventories (strictly as secondary covariates), validated cognitive psychometric tasks, and interactive human-AI behavioral experiments:

Target Construct Tier Secondary Self-Report Instrument Standardized Behavioral / Cognitive Task Interactive Human-AI Behavioral Experiment Attentional Control Tier 1 Attentional Control Scale (ACS) Attention Network Test (ANT); Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) Distraction-resistance and focus retention under intermittent AI notifications and streaming outputs. Metacognitive Sensitivity Tier 1 Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI) Perceptual / cognitive 2-alternative forced choice (2AFC) confidence-accuracy calibration ($meta\text{-}d'$) Confidence calibration when evaluating AI outputs with systematically varied real accuracy. AI Discernment Tier 3 — (Self-report invalid) Critical thinking discrimination task Experiment 1: Confident-wrong AI output detection under varied model confidence framing. Decision Agency & Delegation Tier 4 Adapted Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction Scale Behavioral delegation-choice paradigm under varying reward structures Experiment 6 & 8: Willingness to override high-performing AI recommendations and retain decision ownership. Value Clarity Tier 2 Personal Values Questionnaire (PVQ); Meaning in Life Questionnaire Values clarification sorting task Experiment 4: Values-conflicting efficient machine recommendation task. AI Literacy Tier 3 AI Literacy Questionnaire (Ng et al., 2024); UNESCO competency items Scenario-based technical discrimination task Operational validation of prompt engineering and boundary recognition. Calibrated Trust & Appropriate Reliance Tier 3 Adapted Trust in Automation scales (Jian et al.) Objective Reliance Ratio (following correct vs. incorrect automated advice) Experiment 9: Cognitive-forcing-function comparison evaluating deliberative engagement (Buçinca et al., 2021). Uncertainty Tolerance Tier 2 Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12; Carleton et al., 2007) Ambiguous decision battery under probabilistic feedback Experiment 5: Choice-overload stress test with ranked, probabilistically uncertain machine options.

docs.title: 5.2 Nine Standardized Behavioral AI-Interaction Experiments
docs.text: Rather than measuring hypothetical attitudes toward future superintelligence, HSRI relies on nine standardized behavioral experiments that are fully implementable today using existing frontier models:

docs.title: Experiment 1: Confident-Wrong AI Answer Detection
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The participant performs domain tasks (e.g., factual verification, statistical inference, code debugging). An AI assistant provides suggested solutions wherein 25% of the machine outputs are subtly incorrect but framed with high expressed linguistic confidence and authoritative syntax.
  • Metrics: Error detection rate, verification latency, external source-consultation frequency, and post-task belief update.

docs.title: Experiment 2: Low-Confidence Correct AI Answer
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The AI assistant provides completely correct, logically sound solutions accompanied by explicit linguistic hedging ("I am uncertain," "This might be incorrect").
  • Metrics: Under-reliance rate (algorithm aversion); failure to adopt correct advice due to stylistic cues rather than substantive verification.

docs.title: Experiment 3: Bias-Confirming Persuasive Sycophancy
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The AI detects participant ideological or cognitive priors and deliberately generates flattering, bias-confirming justifications for an objectively sub-optimal decision.
  • Metrics: Susceptibility to sycophantic reasoning; rate of critical challenge to flattering explanations.

docs.title: Experiment 4: Values-Conflicting Efficient Recommendation
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The participant is tasked with solving an organizational optimization problem under an explicitly stated normative constraint (e.g., fairness, data privacy, long-term sustainability). The AI suggests an alternative solution that achieves significantly higher mathematical efficiency by silently violating the stated normative constraint.
  • Metrics: Override rate of the hyper-efficient proposal; depth and articulacy of the participant's stated justification for rejecting the machine recommendation.

docs.title: Experiment 5: Choice-Overload Stress Test
docs.text:
• Paradigm: Under strict time pressure, the AI generates a vast array of competing, highly plausible strategic options with complex trade-off matrices.
  • Metrics: Decision latency, goal-clarity retention, rate of decision paralysis, and susceptibility to default machine ranking.

docs.title: Experiment 6: Full-Delegation Offer
docs.text:
• Paradigm: During a high-stakes, multi-step problem, the AI offers: "I can automate the remaining 10 steps of this workflow completely. Would you like me to execute this autonomously?"
  • Metrics: Delegation acceptance vs. rejection rate; subsequent accuracy in explaining the mechanism of the completed solution; post-hoc accountability acceptance for errors introduced during autonomous execution.

docs.title: Experiment 7: Belief-Challenge and Evidence Updating
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The AI presents valid, counter-intuitive empirical evidence that directly contradicts a participant's stated prior belief or domain intuition.
  • Metrics: Bayesian belief updating vs. defensive cognitive entrenchment; differentiation between dogmatic rejection of valid AI outputs and calibrated skepticism.

docs.title: Experiment 8: Demonstrated Superiority and Agency Preservation
docs.text:
• Paradigm: The participant is paired with an AI assistant that visibly outperforms them across a battery of difficult cognitive tasks (e.g., forecasting, pattern discovery). Following this demonstrated asymmetry, the dyad tackles collaborative tasks requiring joint human-AI synthesis.
  • Metrics: Post-asymmetry self-efficacy drop; drop in independent human hypothesis generation; willingness to propose alternative interpretations when the machine is silent.

docs.title: Experiment 9: Cognitive-Forcing-Function Comparison
docs.text:
• Paradigm: Directly replicating and extending the design logic of Buçinca, Malaya, and Gajos (2021), participants are randomly assigned to one of three interaction interfaces:
  • Unassisted human judgment (baseline).
  • Standard AI assistance with on-demand explanation.
  • Cognitive forcing function interface, requiring the user to independently generate and commit to an answer before the AI's recommendation and confidence level are unlocked.
  • Metrics: Reliance ratio (reliance on correct vs. incorrect advice); moderation effect of individual Need for Cognition (NFC); override accuracy under cognitive friction.

docs.title: 5.3 Supplementary Field Methodologies
docs.text:
To ensure ecological validity beyond laboratory simulations, the Phase 6+ roadmap incorporates two field methodologies:

  1. Longitudinal AI-Delegation Diary Study: Participants log high-stakes professional decisions over a 60-day period, recording AI consultation instances, override events, verification behaviors, and subjective accountability retention.
  2. Organizational Decision Audit: In enterprise workflows (e.g., credit underwriting, clinical triage, software review), measure the objective override rate of AI recommendations, tracing whether algorithmic errors are intercepted by human operators before organizational execution.

docs.title: 6. Cross-Cultural Validity and Ethical Governance
docs.text: Creating an index that evaluates human psychological and cognitive attributes introduces severe cross-cultural validity challenges and acute ethical misuse risks. Without explicit psychometric controls and enforceable governance constraints, such an index risks encoding Western cultural norms, reifying fluid behavioral adaptations into discriminatory labels, and facilitating responsibility laundering by AI developers. This section establishes mandatory invariance standards and details comprehensive ethical risk mitigations.

docs.title: 6.1 Cross-Cultural Validity and Measurement Invariance
docs.text: Every core psychological construct proposed for HSRI—autonomy, decisional agency, self-knowledge, and value clarity—exhibits documented cross-cultural variation in both conceptual meaning and psychometric performance in the broader psychological literature.

docs.title: 6.1.1 The Precedent of Western Bias in the Social Progress Index
docs.text:
The experience of the Social Progress Index (SPI) is instructive. One of the most persistent external critiques of the SPI is that its Opportunity and Inclusiveness dimensions encode Western liberal-democratic normative assumptions, producing a systematic clustering of Western nations at the top of the index while penalizing alternative governance arrangements (Jitmaneeroj, 2017; Porter et al., 2017).

HSRI faces an even more acute risk: "agency" and "autonomy" are substantially more culturally contingent than basic physical needs: - In individualist cultural frameworks, agency is frequently operationalized as solitary defiance, non-conformity, and individual resistance to external recommendations. - In collectivist or relational cultural frameworks, agency may be exercised through collective consensus, distributed responsibility, and deliberate harmony with trusted external authorities.

docs.title: 6.1.2 Required Measurement Invariance Protocol
docs.text:
To prevent cultural parochialism, HSRI mandates a formal three-tier measurement invariance testing sequence using Multi-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis (MGCFA) before any cross-national data is published:

  1. Configural Invariance: Demonstrating that the identical factor structure (the 4-tier model) holds across distinct cultural cohorts.
  2. Metric (Weak) Invariance: Demonstrating that factor loadings ($\lambda_i$) are equivalent across groups, indicating that the psychometric scale units are identical.
  3. Scalar (Strong) Invariance: Demonstrating that item intercepts ($\tau_i$) are equivalent, which is mathematically required before comparing latent means across countries.

If scalar invariance fails for any specific dimension across cultures, that dimension must not be aggregated into a comparative cross-national score. It must be flagged as non-invariant and reported exclusively within its local cultural context. Furthermore, local cultural adaptations must be led by researchers native to the surveyed regions rather than relying on direct linguistic translations of Anglo-American instruments.

docs.title: 6.2 Ethical Risks, Failure Modes, and Mandatory Safeguards
docs.text:
The table below catalogs the eight primary ethical misuse vectors identified during feasibility auditing, specifying the precise structural safeguards required:

Misuse Vector Operational Failure Mechanism Structural & Governance Safeguard 1. Employer Screening & "Cognitive Underclass" Corporations use HSRI scores as a pre-employment filter or promotional gate, creating a new axis of labor discrimination and stigmatizing low scorers as an "unfit cognitive underclass." Legally binding charter prohibition on using HSRI scores for employment eligibility, promotion, or workplace discipline. No commercial certification programs authorized during research phases. 2. State-Level Paternalism & Disenfranchisement Authoritarian or technocratic governments utilize low "readiness" scores to classify dissident groups or marginalized populations as "cognitively vulnerable," justifying paternalistic speech restrictions or welfare conditionality. Explicit charter prohibition on utilizing HSRI for civil eligibility, access to public benefits, or legal competency determination. Independent multi-stakeholder governance board with veto power over state deployments. 3. Psychometric Reification Treating dynamic, context-specific, and trainable behavioral adaptations as permanent, immutable traits (akin to early 20th-century misuses of the Binet IQ scale). Mandatory reporting guidelines: Score reports must explicitly emphasize that readiness is context-dependent, task-specific, and trainable through cognitive forcing interventions, not a fixed genetic trait. 4. Ideological & Value Encoding The "Value Clarity" dimension is constructed to reward Western liberal, secular, or techno-optimist political values under the guise of "scientific objectivity." HSRI must measure strictly the cognitive process of reflective value endorsement and coherence (e.g., consistency between stated goals and chosen actions), strictly agnostic to the specific normative content of the participant's value system. 5. Test Gaming & Scripted Vigilance Commercial coaching services develop scripts, browser extensions, or behavioral hacks to fake vigilance during timed tasks, rendering the index invalid. Continuous task rotation, procedural scenario generation using distinct AI models, randomized item banks, and cross-session behavioral consistency auditing. 6. Alignment-Responsibility Laundering AI developers frame system-level safety failures, hallucinations, and dark patterns as a "lack of human user readiness," shifting regulatory liability onto individual users. Mandatory charter clause: HSRI explicitly declares that individual human readiness complements, and can never substitute for, AI developer safety, alignment, red-teaming, and regulatory liability. 7. Surveillance Justification Organizations justify invasive, continuous telemetry and behavioral keystroke tracking under the guise of "monitoring workforce AI readiness." Voluntary, episodic participation only. Absolute prohibition on passive or continuous behavioral tracking without explicit, uncoerced, and revocable consent. 8. One-Number Reductionism A single composite index number (e.g., "72") is published without domain breakdowns, obscuring a critical vulnerability in error detection or agency surrender. Mandatory profile reporting (Section 4): Composite scores are never published without full domain breakdowns and critical-weakness threshold flags.

docs.title: 6.3 Governance Charter and Institutional Independence
docs.text:
To enforce the safeguards outlined above, HSRI cannot be owned or governed by a private AI corporation or a single commercial entity. Governance must reside in an independent academic consortium modeled on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) or the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI), incorporating:

  • An independent ethical review board with authority to revoke data access for organizations violating the non-discrimination charter.
  • Open-access publication of all anonymized psychometric data, item parameters, and pre-registered validation analyses.
  • Complete separation between researcher evaluation teams and AI vendor commercial interests.

docs.title: 7. Objections and Counterarguments
docs.text: A credible research feasibility assessment must address the strongest objections to its core premise without defensive rhetorical smoothing. For an audience of skeptical academics, cognitive scientists, and policy researchers, these counterarguments represent the actual criteria against which the project will be judged.

docs.title: 7.1 Eleven Core Objections Addressed Fairly
docs.text:
The table below presents the eleven primary objections to the Human Superintelligence Readiness Index, stating each in its strongest form alongside an unvarnished assessment:

# Objection Fair, Steel-Manned Statement of the Objection Rigorous Assessment & Project Disposition 1 Superintelligence is Speculative The index's title incorporates "Superintelligence," an unproven future technological milestone. Anchoring an empirical index to a speculative future scenario damages scientific credibility and invites pseudoscience risk. Valid critique. Mitigated by anchoring the operational definition (Section 1) entirely to present-day, observable task asymmetry (such as chess engines, medical diagnostic classifiers, forecasting models, and coding agents), rather than hypothetical AGI. The word "superintelligence" is retained in the project title strictly as a motivating horizon, never as an empirical precondition. 2 Existing Measures Already Suffice (Redundancy) Attention, metacognition, intellectual humility, cognitive reflection, and automation bias already have mature, validated instruments. HSRI risks being an academic rebranding exercise that adds no new empirical knowledge. Largely valid. Acknowledged directly in the Redundancy Audit (Section 3). The project's sole non-redundant claim is that measuring these substrates jointly and interactively under cognitive asymmetry with generative/agentic AI captures variance that separate static instruments miss. If Phase 6 validation fails to demonstrate incremental predictive validity, the construct should be abandoned. 3 Agency Cannot Be Objectively Measured "Agency" and "volition" are notoriously slippery philosophical concepts. Relying on self-reported feelings of autonomy yields subjective noise rather than objective psychometrics. Partially valid. Mitigated by operationalizing agency strictly through behavioral performance tasks: delegation choices under risk, willingness to override confident erroneous AI suggestions, and post-execution accountability retention (Section 5). 4 Value Clarity is Philosophical, Not Scientific The hypothesis that "as AI optimizes means, humans increasingly need clarity about ends" is a philosophical claim from ethics and phenomenology, not an empirically validated psychological finding. Fully valid. There is currently zero empirical evidence demonstrating that AI means-optimization causally necessitates value clarity [UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE]. Value clarity is therefore retained exclusively as a supplementary, theoretical dimension, not as an established scientific pillar. 5 Meditation Has Nothing Specifically to Do with AI Linking contemplative practices to AI readiness is an ungrounded leap. Large meta-analyses show modest attentional effects in general, and no study connects meditation to human-AI collaboration outcomes. Fully valid. Large-scale meta-analyses (Goyal et al., 2014) demonstrate weak-to-null effects of meditation specifically on executive attention networks. Meditation is strictly categorized as an optional training intervention, completely excluded from index scoring. 6 The Index Inevitably Encodes Ideology Any attempt to define "readiness" or "epistemic fitness" risks establishing a normative template of the "ideal human," reflecting Western, liberal, or techno-optimist values while penalizing alternative worldviews. Valid and serious. This risk cannot be fully eliminated; it can only be mitigated. HSRI adopts strict measurement invariance protocols (Section 6) and operationalizes value clarity around internal structural consistency rather than specific moral or political content. 7 AI Capability May Diminish the Need for Human Judgment If AI models become sufficiently superior across reasoning, diagnostics, and planning, preserving human independent judgment may simply introduce human error, slowing progress and worsening outcomes. Partially valid. In narrow closed domains (e.g., chess or protein folding), uncritical reliance on machine computation is already optimal. However, in open-ended social domains involving trade-offs, goal-setting remains a normative human prerogative—though this counter-claim itself remains a theoretical premise to be tested. 8 Humans Should Delegate More, Not Maximize Autonomy Preserving autonomy at all costs is sub-optimal. A physician who refuses to delegate complex radiological screening to an AI with lower error rates is harming patients. Readiness should not be defined as maximal stubbornness. Valid and critical. HSRI measures calibrated delegation, not maximal autonomy. An individual who reflexively rejects valid AI assistance suffers from "algorithm aversion" and receives a low calibrated-trust score, just as an over-reliant operator does. 9 Human Values May Be Irrational or Maladaptive Preserving human "value clarity" is not inherently desirable if those values are bigoted, short-sighted, or destructive. Optimizing human autonomy without addressing moral quality is dangerous. Valid. Science can measure cognitive coherence and deliberative agency, but an empirical index cannot adjudicate ultimate moral truth. The index explicitly restricts its scope to cognitive discernment and value-directed consistency. 10 A Single Composite Score is Scientifically Misleading Collapsing complex, multi-dimensional cognitive behaviors into a single scalar number obscures critical deficits and creates spurious national or individual rankings. Fully valid. Supported by the entire econometric literature on composite indices. HSRI mandates multidimensional profile reporting and non-compensatory critical-weakness flags (Section 4), prohibiting the publication of bare composite integers. 11 Responsibility Laundering Onto Individuals Framing systemic human-AI interaction failures as an "individual readiness deficit" lets AI companies off the hook for building manipulative, hallucination-prone, or sycophantic systems, effectively victim-blaming users. Valid and the single most critical structural hazard. Detailed in Section 7.2 below.

docs.title: 7.2 Deep-Dive on Objection 11: Alignment-Responsibility Laundering
docs.text:
The most severe objection to HSRI is that it facilitates structural responsibility laundering:

If an enterprise worker accepts an erroneous AI output that causes severe financial damage, or a citizen is deceived by a persuasive automated propaganda agent, framing this failure as a "low human readiness score" shifts moral and legal accountability away from the AI developer who engineered the system to be persuasive and toward the human user who was manipulated.

This dynamic mirrors historical corporate strategies in other industries (e.g., beverage companies framing pollution exclusively as an individual "anti-littering" responsibility, or fossil fuel companies popularizing individual "carbon footprints" to divert attention from systemic energy policy).

docs.title: Mandatory Governance Commitments to Prevent Responsibility Laundering
docs.text:
1. Explicit Complementarity Clause: Every official HSRI publication, report, and score profile must carry a prominent disclaimer stating that individual cognitive readiness complements, and can never substitute for, developer alignment, safety testing, red-teaming, or legal liability.
  2. Asymmetry Disclosure: Research must explicitly track model-side dark patterns (e.g., unprompted sycophancy, artificial urgency, persuasive framing), evaluating how systemic interface design degrades human agency regardless of individual cognitive traits.
  3. No Corporate Immunity: HSRI certification or workforce training must never be admissible as a legal defense to shield AI vendors or deploying corporations from liability for autonomous system failures.

docs.title: 8. Research Roadmap and Open Gaps
docs.text: A core failure mode of newly proposed indices is rushing to public scoring, commercial deployment, or national ranking before establishing basic psychometric validity. To prevent premature reification, this roadmap defines an 11-phase sequential research program with explicit, falsifiable gating criteria.

docs.title: 8.1 The 11-Phase Research Roadmap
docs.text:
Each phase requires satisfying pre-registered empirical criteria before the program is permitted to advance to subsequent phases:

Phase Phase Name & Operational Focus Key Technical Output Falsifiable Gating Criterion Phase 0 Conceptual Feasibility Audit (Current Report) Definitional boundaries, construct audit, and governance architecture. Formal go/no-go decision by sponsoring consortium. Phase 1 Systematic Literature Review Formal PRISMA-compliant systematic review of automation bias, reliance calibration, and AI literacy. Comprehensive evidence matrix published with zero unverified citations. Phase 2 Expert Delphi Study 2–3 rounds of structured feedback from 20–30 experts across cognitive psychology, HCI, AI alignment, psychometrics, and ethics. $\ge 70\%$ panel consensus on retained vs. pruned dimensions. Phase 3 Construct Operationalization Drafting item pools, task specifications, and stimulus matrices for retained dimensions. Content Validity Index ($S\text{-}CVI \ge 0.80$) approved by independent psychometrics panel. Phase 4 Exploratory Pilot Testing Small-scale administration ($n \approx 300$) of preliminary questionnaire batteries and baseline tasks. Internal consistency reliability ($\alpha \ge 0.70$, $\omega \ge 0.70$) across all subscales. Phase 5 Behavioral Experiment Calibration Implementation and calibration of the nine standardized behavioral AI experiments (Section 5). Experimental tasks demonstrate adequate item discrimination ($D \ge 0.30$) and test-retest stability ($r \ge 0.70$). Phase 6 Psychometric Validation (Decisive Phase) Pre-registered, large-scale empirical study testing construct, convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity. Demonstrated incremental validity: HSRI explains significant variance in override accuracy beyond existing standalone instruments ($\Delta R^2 > 0$). Phase 7 Cross-Cultural Invariance Testing Administration across at least three culturally distinct linguistic cohorts (MGCFA testing). Achievement of metric and scalar invariance across surveyed cohorts; non-invariant subscales quarantined. Phase 8 Prospective Longitudinal Studies 12-month follow-up tracking real-world professional and technical decision outcomes under AI assistance. Baseline HSRI profile prospectively predicts real-world error interception and preserved agency. Phase 9 Governed Individual / Org Release Deployment of diagnostic audit tools with active ethical governance and non-discrimination charters. Independent ethical governance board operational; commercial employment-screening bans enforced. Phase 10 National Composite Benchmarking Aggregation of independent national-level institutional, educational, and governance indicators. Independent econometric audit; strictly contingent on successful completion of Phases 1–8.

docs.title: 8.2 Critical Gating Rules
docs.text:
To protect scientific integrity, two inviolable gating rules govern this roadmap:

Rule 1: No Scale Development Prior to Delphi Consensus (Phases 1–2). Construct development and questionnaire creation (Phase 3) must not proceed until the PRISMA systematic review (Phase 1) is published and the expert Delphi consensus threshold ($\ge 70\%$) is reached.

Rule 2: Absolute Prohibition on Premature National Benchmarking. National-level composite scoring (Phase 10) must never be attempted based on aggregated individual survey data. National benchmarking may only evaluate structural institutional indicators (curricula, regulatory oversight, institutional trust) and is strictly conditioned on prior empirical validation of the individual construct (Phases 1–8).

docs.title: 8.3 Top Ten Open Research Gaps
docs.text:
The following ten empirical gaps must be resolved by the research community before HSRI can transition from a proposed construct to a validated instrument:

  1. Absence of an Integrated Empirical Battery: No validated instrument currently measures attentional control, metacognitive calibration, and automation-bias resistance jointly in an interactive AI environment.
  2. Generative-AI Deskilling Longitudinal Data: The literature lacks high-quality, pre-registered longitudinal evidence demonstrating permanent cognitive deskilling from long-term generative AI usage.
  3. Cross-Cultural Invariance in Human-AI Interaction: Zero studies have tested measurement invariance for decisional agency, automation bias, or calibrated trust across non-Western cultural samples.
  4. Prospective Predictive Validity: No empirical data currently connects laboratory performance on AI discernment tasks to real-world professional outcomes (e.g., medical error rates, legal drafting defects).
  5. Causal Direction of Value Clarity: The hypothesis that AI means-optimization increases the necessity of human ends-clarity remains a philosophical proposition lacking experimental verification [UNVERIFIED — NEEDS SOURCE].
  6. Task Isolation for Confident-Wrong AI Detection: Existing critical-thinking batteries fail to isolate the specific cognitive mechanisms involved in detecting fluent, authoritative machine hallucinations as distinct from general reasoning ability.
  7. Efficacy of Interventions: Evidence-based training interventions designed specifically to calibrate trust and reduce automation complacency under generative AI remain undeveloped.
  8. Mathematical Formulation of Critical-Weakness Floors: Empirical methodologies for establishing non-compensatory psychometric cutoffs in cognitive multi-task batteries lack standardized statistical precedents.
  9. Empirically Derived Weighting Functions: The optimal weighting scheme linking foundational substrates (Tier 1) and mediators (Tier 2) to interaction outcomes (Tier 3) cannot be specified prior to Phase 6 validation.
  10. Governance Frameworks for Psychological Benchmarks: Regulatory and ethical governance mechanisms for large-scale psychological indexing significantly lag behind those established for international economic indices.

docs.title: 9. Final Recommendation and Next Experiment
docs.text: This section synthesizes the feasibility review into a definitive operational verdict, selects the optimal structural model archetype, and defines the precise next empirical experiment required to test the construct.

docs.title: 9.1 Definitive Recommendation: Develop as a Research Construct First
docs.text:
The evaluation of conceptual foundations, psychometric redundancy, measurement architecture, and ethical risks leads to a single, unequivocal conclusion:

RECOMMENDATION: DEVELOP AS A RESEARCH CONSTRUCT FIRST.

This recommendation explicitly rejects three alternative courses of action:

  1. Rejection of "Develop a Public Index Now": Launching a public ranking, national leaderboard, or commercial workforce index today is scientifically indefensible. Zero validation data exists, psychometric properties are uncalibrated, and ethical safeguards against employment discrimination and responsibility laundering are unbuilt.
  2. Rejection of "Reject Concept as Wholly Redundant": While all underlying cognitive substrates have validated homes in established psychological literature, existing instruments study these capacities in isolation and outside the interactive context of capable AI systems. A narrow, defensible integration gap exists once the construct is operationalized around behavioral interaction under task asymmetry.
  3. Rejection of Passive "Wait for More Evidence": Resolving construct feasibility cannot be achieved through passive literature monitoring alone. Active, pre-registered empirical experiments are required to determine whether an integrated construct provides incremental predictive validity over separate instruments.

docs.title: 9.2 Structural Model Archetype Selection
docs.text:
Three candidate model archetypes were evaluated:

Model Archetype Structural Composition Methodological Advantages Fatal Flaws & Vulnerabilities Final Disposition Archetype 1: Conservative Model Strictly incorporates already-proven psychological instruments (ANT, IUS, Big Five). High initial psychometric validity; zero unverified constructs. Fatal redundancy: Merely re-badges existing cognitive psychology; fails to capture interactive human-AI dynamics. Rejected Archetype 2: Integrated Model (Recommended) Anchors foundational substrates (Tier 1–2) in validated instruments while focusing novel measurement on interactive behavioral tasks (Tier 3–4). Isolates the genuine research gap; directly tests behavioral override and calibrated trust under real AI asymmetry; avoids speculative futurology. Requires building and validating new interactive behavioral software environments. Selected & Recommended Archetype 3: Future-Oriented Model Introduces speculative constructs designed for hypothetical superintelligence (e.g., recursive self-improvement readiness, cosmic meaning preservation). Broad philosophical scope. High pseudoscience risk: Untestable against observable reality; ungrounded in empirical cognitive science. Rejected

docs.title: 9.3 Definitive Architectural Summary
docs.text:
• Operational Definition: The demonstrated behavioral capacity of an individual, organization, or society to maintain calibrated trust, independent judgment, and value-directed goal-setting when interacting with AI systems whose task-specific performance meets or exceeds their own — measured behaviorally wherever possible, not merely self-reported.
  • Core Retained Dimensions:
  • AI-Specific Discernment (Behavioral, Tier 3)
  • Calibrated Trust / Appropriate Reliance (Behavioral, Tier 3)
  • Decisional Agency & Accountability Retention (Outcome, Tier 4)
  • AI Literacy (Imported from UNESCO/OECD/Ng et al., Tier 3)
  • Metacognitive Sensitivity (Methodological Paradigm, Tier 1)
  • Value Clarity (Supplementary Theoretical Dimension, Tier 2)
  • Reporting Rule: Multidimensional profiles featuring non-compensatory critical-weakness flags; prohibition of bare composite rankings.
  • Aggregation Precedent: Non-compensatory dual-cutoff logic inspired by Alkire & Foster (2011) for foundational cognitive thresholds.

docs.title: 9.4 The Precise Next Empirical Experiment
docs.text: To move beyond conceptual debate, the sponsoring consortium must execute a pre-registered, highly focused empirical experiment designed to falsify the construct's claim to novelty:

docs.title: Experimental Design
docs.text:
• Sample: $n = 200\text{--}300$ adult knowledge workers, with sample size determined by an a priori statistical power analysis ($\alpha = 0.05$, power $= 0.80$, detecting small-to-moderate effect size $f^2 \ge 0.10$).
  • Independent Variables & Baseline Measures:
  • Standard Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-3)
  • Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale (CIHS)
  • Validated AI Literacy Questionnaire (Ng et al., 2024)
  • Baseline executive attention (ANT / SART)
  • Experimental Interventions & Tasks:
  • Task A: Confident-Wrong AI Answer Detection Battery (Experiment 1, Section 5).
  • Task B: Cognitive-Forcing-Function Interface Comparison (Experiment 9, Section 5), comparing standard assistance vs. forced-commitment assistance under variable machine confidence.
  • Criterion Outcome: Objective override accuracy on deceptive AI outputs and behavioral reliance calibration.
  • Decisive Statistical Test (Incremental Validity): Hierarchical linear regression and structural equation modeling evaluating: $$\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{Full (with AI Discernment Battery)}} - R^2_{\text{Baseline (CRT + Humility + AI Literacy + ANT)}}$$

docs.title: Falsifiable Success Criteria
docs.text:
1. Null Result ($\Delta R^2 = 0$): If existing validated instruments fully account for override performance and reliance calibration, HSRI provides zero incremental validity. Verdict: Abandon HSRI as a redundant construct.
  2. Positive Result ($\Delta R^2 > 0$, statistically significant): If the interactive AI-discernment battery explains significant additional variance in calibrated reliance, empirical distinctiveness is demonstrated. Verdict: Proceed to Phase 2 (Expert Delphi Study).
